newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-ENGLAND CONTINUE SEARCH FOR MATCH-WINNING BOWLER.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ENGLAND CONTINUE SEARCH FOR MATCH-WINNING BOWLER.

text.p: Nestled against the cricket scoreboards and fixtures on the sports pages of a leading British newspaper, one advertisement stands out like a beacon.
"The search is on this summer for the next generation of strike bowlers...You don't have to be a cricketer, just big and strong and reckon you can...Bowl Quick!"
The advert spells out the desperate shortage of strike bowlers in English cricket since their last world-class fast bowler, Bob Willis, hung up his boots 13 years ago.
It is now 10 years since England last won an Ashes series and there is still little to suggest they can field an attack this year capable of dismissing the Australian tourists twice.

The primary worry of the new England selection panel before the six-test Ashes series will be the mental and physical state of Dominic Cork, so effective in his debut series against the West Indies two years ago and so ineffectual on the winter tour of Zimbabwe and New Zealand.
Cork lost his late outswinger, appeared to be straining for pace and is anyway currently injured and unlikely to play in the one-day series this month.
Darren Gough, who experienced his own fall from grace after a successful tour of Australia in 1994-95, bounced back during the winter.
Enthusiastic, with a wicked bouncer and steep in-ducker, Gough's slinging action makes it unlikely he will ever command consistent control of line and length.
He is though, England's one prospective match-winner, if the selectors decide against another chance for 34-year-old Devon Malcolom.
Glamorgan off-spinner Robert Croft impressed in Zimbabwe and New Zealand, but even in his most successful county season last year still conceded 30 runs a wicket.
The shortage of fast bowlers in English cricket is nothing new. What must be of equal concern to the selectors is the shortage of old-fashioned line-and-length bowlers.

Angus Fraser, apparently no longer required for national duty, can at least be guaranteed to put six consecutive balls on the same side of the pitch. Few others, including Andrew Caddick who is likely to open the bowling with Gough, instill the same confidence.
England's chief hope of putting pressure on Australia rests with an undeniably talented batting lineup.
Alec Stewart, a throwback to the model professionals who once kept England at the top of the cricketing world, will bat at number three and keep wicket.
Captain Mike Atherton, equally professional in attitude, will open the batting while Graham Thorpe and John Crawley, despite indifferent early season form, are assured of middle-order berths.
Newspaper columns, radio and television programmes and innumerable pub conversations have been devoted over the past month to discussing the state of England's national summer game.
A new chief executive as well as a new selection committee is in place and the perennial optimists find springtime signs that the tide is turning.
But the advertisements and posters seeking a fast bowler for the millennium may unwittingly reveal more than they intend about the lack of structure in the English game beyond the counties.
The final selection will not be made by any of England's former heroes but instead by those old Australian warriors Dennis Lillee and Jeff Thomson.
And the winner, having nowhere to go in England to learn his trade, will win a scholarship to Lillee's fast bowling academy in India.
